summary: This standards-track document describes the conventions for using Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman key agreement with curve25519 and curve448 in the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people can agree on a secret without sharing it. This says how to do that with modern curves in secure messages.

subtitle: How secure messages can use the fast X25519 and X448 curves to agree on a key for each recipient.

tldr.problem: The Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) already supports Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman for some curves, but it had no conventions for curve25519 and curve448.
tldr.mechanism: The sender makes a fresh (ephemeral) key pair on the recipient's curve, combines it with the recipient's static public key, and runs the shared secret through a key derivation function (ANSI-X9.63-KDF or HKDF) to get a key-encryption key that wraps the content key.
tldr.outcome: CMS enveloped-data, authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data messages can now be protected with X25519 or X448, using new object identifiers for the HKDF variants.

today: RFC 8418 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2018. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to the metadata for this site, so it remains the definition of X25519 and X448 key agreement in CMS.

sections.title: What the RFC Covers
sections.content:
RFC 8418 describes how to use Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key agreement with curve25519 and curve448 inside the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). Using curve25519 with Diffie-Hellman is called X25519, and using curve448 is called X448. The curves themselves come from RFC 7748.

Key agreement is supported in three CMS content types: enveloped-data and authenticated-data from RFC 5652, and authenticated-enveloped-data from RFC 5083. Conventions for ECC with other curves are in RFC 5753; the RFC states that those other curves are not deprecated.
sections.plainLanguage: CMS is a standard envelope for secret messages. This RFC adds two new ways to agree on the lock combination for that envelope.

sections.title: Ephemeral-Static Key Agreement
sections.content:
The RFC uses Ephemeral-Static ECDH. The originator MUST generate an ephemeral key pair on the same curve as the recipient's public key, use it for a single CMS-protected content type, and then discard it. The recipient's static public key comes from the recipient's certificate (RFC 5280).

Implementations MUST check whether the computed shared secret is the all-zero value and abort if so. If an implementation uses an alternative to the method in RFC 7748 Section 6, the additional checks in Section 7 of that RFC SHOULD be performed.

The shared secret (called K) is fed to a key derivation function (KDF) together with the wanted length and a DER-encoded ECC-CMS-SharedInfo structure. The output is a pairwise key-encryption key (KEK).

If the optional ukm field is present, it goes into the entityUInfo field. That way a different KEK is generated even if the ephemeral private key is wrongly reused. A ukm MUST be chosen to be unique with very high probability.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender makes a one-time secret just for this message and mixes it with the receiver's public key. Both sides end up with the same secret, and the sender throws theirs away.

sections.title: The Two Key Derivation Functions
sections.content:
Two KDFs are described. ANSI-X9.63-KDF hashes the shared secret K, a 32-bit counter starting at 0x00000001 and the DER-encoded ECC-CMS-SharedInfo. It repeats with an incremented counter until enough material exists, then uses the leftmost portion as the KEK.

HKDF (RFC 5869) works in two steps, HKDF-Extract then HKDF-Expand. If a ukm is provided it is also used as the salt; otherwise HKDF uses an appropriate number of zero octets.

The length of the KEK is used twice. The suppPubInfo field holds it in bits as a 32-bit number in network byte order (for AES-256 that is 0x00000100), while HKDF-Expand takes it in octets.
sections.plainLanguage: The shared secret is like raw dough. A key derivation function kneads it into a key of exactly the right size.

sections.title: How the CMS Content Types Use It
sections.content:
For all three content types the sender generates a random content key (a content-encryption key, an authentication key, or a content-authenticated-encryption key). The KEK wraps that key for each recipient. When there are several recipients, the same key MUST be wrapped for each of them.

For recipients using X25519 or X448, the kari choice of RecipientInfo MUST be used. Within KeyAgreeRecipientInfo:

  • The version MUST be 3.
  • The originatorKey alternative MUST be used and MUST hold the ephemeral key. Its algorithm is id-X25519 or id-X448, and the public key is an OCTET STRING.
  • An X25519 public key is exactly 32 octets and an X448 public key is exactly 56 octets.
  • The recipient is identified either by issuerAndSerialNumber or by the subject key identifier of its certificate.

The authenticated-data and authenticated-enveloped-data sections simply point back to these same KeyAgreeRecipientInfo rules.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message gets a fresh key to lock it. That key is then locked again in a small box for each reader, and only that reader can open their box.

sections.title: Identifiers and Capabilities
sections.content:
X25519 uses object identifier { 1 3 101 110 } and X448 uses { 1 3 101 111 }, assigned in RFC 8410, which also covers carrying these keys in certificates.

The ANSI-X9.63-KDF identifiers come from RFC 5753. This RFC defines three new identifiers under smime-alg for ECDH with HKDF using SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512 (values 19, 20 and 21). Each is used with a parameter naming the key-encryption algorithm, such as AES key wrap.

A sender MAY announce support through the SMIMECapabilities attribute. The RFC lists hexadecimal values for each KDF and hash combined with AES-128 or AES-256 key wrap.
sections.plainLanguage: Every method gets a name tag made of numbers so both sides know exactly which recipe to use.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC mostly defers: readers should consult the security considerations of RFC 5652, RFC 5083 and RFC 7748.

It adds two points. The ephemeral key pair is used once and discarded, so an originator who wants to read their own message later must treat themselves as a recipient. And implementations MUST support processing of the ukm field, so interoperability is not a concern whether it is present or not; when present it ensures a different KEK even if the ephemeral private key is improperly reused.
sections.plainLanguage: The one-time secret must really be one-time. If the sender wants to read the message later, they must add themselves to the guest list.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
IANA assigned one object identifier for the ASN.1 module in Appendix A, id-mod-cms-ecdh-alg-2017, in the S/MIME module identifiers registry. It also assigned the three HKDF key agreement identifiers in the S/MIME algorithms registry.

The appendix itself holds the ASN.1 module that extends the key agreement algorithms and S/MIME capabilities from RFC 5753 with the HKDF variants.
sections.plainLanguage: A registry keeps the official list of name tags, and this RFC asked for a few new ones to be added.
